item.title: Hi Dr Kay, I've been researching the development of the GUI for a project recently and I've been wondering something: why did you feel that windows needed to be able to overlap in the first place? What was wrong with only having them side by side?
item.description: This idea came mainly from struggling with the desire for a bit-map display at all on a personal computer because the cost per bit was very high in 1971, and it was clear that even using every bit for processing, it would be difficult to have enough to do what we wanted it to do. Also, we knew we needed multiple windows/views — from the schemes we liked at Utah — and wanted the user to be able to work on parallel “projects” concurrently (because most people are engaged in more than one during a day). We very much wanted a “universal” display (and line drawing displays didn’t measure up). We realised we could have “poor man’s halftoning” with a one bit per pixel display. We also wanted “2 1/2 D” Disney style “in twos” animation, etc., for the children. If the pixels were small enough we could get high quality text characters because the Modulation Transfer Function of human vision was non-linear in a good direction. The eventual Dynabook display would be flat-and bitmapped, etc. We had all agreed that anything we invented at Parc had to be engineered and constructed for 100 users. So a personal computer design “time-machine” that was really new would be expensive … All of this implied that a desired display we could afford would have a small visual angle. And so forth. This was a “shower-idea”. It occurred to me that if the rendering was “2 1/2 D” generally, then just refreshing a window would seem to bring it to the top, and this would effectively allow a much larger area to be in view. And, that this still allowed windows to be “tiled” if desired. The “time-machine” idea (so that even future hardware would be emulated in SW) led to a very fast (5X main memory microcoded CPU) and this allowed the the maximum tradeoffs for buying DRAM. By the time Chuck Thacker started the Alto project, pretty much everything — visually, auditory, and semantically — had been emulated well enough to allow these to be parametric using the Alto microcode. The full blown combination of features mentioned above was realised in the eventual Smalltalk system by a little bit of “science” (moi) and a lot of brilliant software engineering (for which Dan Ingalls should get the main recognition).

item.title: Who is Alan Kay and why did he call himself "the father of object oriented programming"?
item.description: I never called myself “the father of OOP”. I did coin the term for a general style that was being developed by a number of people, including Ivan Sutherland, Dahl & Nygaard, myself, etc. The term “OOP” was a hasty and poor choice on my part. I should have called it something more like “Process Oriented Programming”, etc. Sorry. David L Smith in a comment below said: Well, I think that might have confused people since we’re all familiar with running “processes” but “objects” had less concrete usage. My reply should have been here: Back in the 60s “objects” generally meant “something with multiple fields (including possible procedure pointers)” and this is what Sketchpad, AED, etc. had. LISP’s early use of the term “object” more or less meant this semantically (something with “properties” (some of which could be lambda expressions). Simula used independent Algol-60 blocks (which had variables that could hold data or signify procedures …). My thought — catalysed by Sketchpad and Simula — was that the intercommunicating “processes” starting to be used by time-sharing and multiprocessing — were a great semantic primitive for “everything”, but that it would take a lot of software engineering to make them pragmatically universal. When someone asked me what I was working on, I said without thinking “OOP”, instead of how I was actually thinking about it (which included trying to not think in terms of passive data structures or the simulation of them).

item.title: Did the ENIAC have a BIOS?
item.description: I’m pretty sure it nether had a BIOS, nor anything analogous to a BIOS. I’m on the side of those who don’t consider it to be a stored program computer (there were a few tricks you could do along those lines, but not enough IMO to qualify). An interesting question is whether the program needed for “Basic IO” needs to be in firmware to qualify (the letter of the law says “yes”, but I’m more with the spirit of the law, which doesn’t need a ROM to qualify). Along the spirit lines, it’s worth contemplating that well into the 60s, many computers were started “cold” with no code at all, but by first using toggles or other kinds of switches, an operator would key in a few instructions that would e.g. read in a paper taper full of more instructions. This was the case for most of the early DEC computers. The CDC 6600 ca 1964–5 had a panel of switches for initial cold starts (this was much more convenient than toggles …). Turning to Wikipedia, it says that the first officially named BIOS happened in 1975 for the CP/M OS, but that the “modern” version of the term was ca 1981 for the IBM PC. Both of these were ROM based.
